<margin>Having an intention to practice virtue is the thief of virtue.</margin>
<margin>If one labors their mind over trivial matters between the eyebrows, virtue is even more compromised.</margin>

<margin>From this, looking back at the mind, it is chaotic and turbulent; it can never attain virtue or progress toward the Dao.</margin>

<unclear>Harmonizing</unclear> with these, there is no greater thief of virtue than having a deliberate intention, and the mind has its own "eyelashes" <note>a metaphor for trivial, immediate distractions</note>. When the mind becomes obsessed with these, one looks inward; by looking inward <note>in the sense of self-conscious introspection rather than natural observation</note>, one suffers ruin. <summary>This passage discusses the importance of humility and the danger of deliberate, self-conscious morality, contrasting the modest behavior of Zheng Kaofu with the arrogance of those who misuse their rank.</summary>
